entities.name: Apollinaris of Ravenna
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Apollinaris of Ravenna, a pivotal figure in the nascent Christianization of the western Roman Empire, is revered as the proto-bishop and patron saint of Ravenna, Italy. Though historical details are often veiled in hagiographical tradition, he is firmly established as a Syrian missionary martyred around 79 CE, during the reign of Vespasian. His mission laid the foundational ecclesiastical structure for one of late antiquity's most significant cities, transforming it into a beacon of Christian faith and a future capital.

Tradition recounts that Apollinaris, a disciple of Saint Peter, was sent from Antioch to evangelize the region of Emilia-Romagna. Upon arriving in Classis, the strategic port of Ravenna, he established the first Christian community, enduring severe persecutions under Roman authorities for his unwavering commitment to the new faith. Accounts describe him healing the sick, casting out demons, and converting numerous pagans, which incited the wrath of local officials. His ministry was punctuated by multiple arrests, tortures, and exiles, ultimately culminating in his glorious martyrdom, likely by beating or decapitation, outside Ravenna around 79 CE.

Apollinaris's enduring legacy is intrinsically linked to the rise of Ravenna as a powerful ecclesiastical and political center in the 5th and 6th centuries. His veneration fostered the construction of magnificent churches, most notably the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, consecrated in 549 CE, which stands as a monumental testament to his cult and the golden age of Byzantine art in Italy. The diocese he founded became an influential archdiocese, wielding significant spiritual and temporal power throughout the medieval period, ensuring the continued spread and consolidation of Christianity in northern Italy. His narrative served as a powerful model of apostolic fortitude and missionary zeal for centuries.
